items.followUp: Why were fungi once grouped with plants, and what feature distinguishes them from plants?

rubric.why: Gives a plant-like feature that led some biologists to place fungi in Plantae.
rubric.description: Fungi have cell walls and do not move from place to place.

rubric.why: Identifies the key difference from plants that caused disagreement.
rubric.description: Fungi lack chlorophyll and obtain food heterotrophically rather than photosynthesizing.
rubric.how: Award for both the lack of chlorophyll and heterotrophic nutrition.

modelAnswer: Some biologists placed fungi in kingdom Plantae because they have cell walls and are non-motile.
Others disagreed because fungi lack chlorophyll and are heterotrophic; they cannot make their own food by photosynthesis.

items.followUp: Describe what happens to the cell membrane and cell contents during apoptosis.

rubric.why: Defines blebs as a feature of the cell membrane during apoptosis.
rubric.description: Blebs are bubble-like bulges of the cell membrane formed during apoptosis.
rubric.how: Award for describing the membrane bulges.

rubric.why: Defines apoptotic bodies as fragments produced from the dying cell.
rubric.description: Apoptotic bodies are membrane-enclosed fragments of a cell undergoing apoptosis, which can be engulfed by other cells.
rubric.how: Award for identifying them as fragments and indicating their membrane enclosure or engulfment.

modelAnswer: Blebs are bubble-like bulges that form on the cell membrane during apoptosis.
Apoptotic bodies are membrane-enclosed fragments of the dying cell; they are engulfed by other cells.

items.followUp: What separates during anaphase II, and what happens to the centromeres?

rubric.why: Identifies the structures that separate and their movement.
rubric.description: Homologous chromosomes separate and move towards opposite poles of the cell.
rubric.how: Award for both separation of homologous chromosomes and movement to opposite poles.

rubric.why: Distinguishes anaphase I from the separation of chromatids in mitosis or anaphase II.
rubric.description: Centromeres do not divide, so sister chromatids remain joined.
rubric.how: Award for stating that centromeres do not split or that sister chromatids remain together.

modelAnswer: Homologous chromosomes separate and move towards opposite poles of the cell.
The centromeres do not divide, so sister chromatids remain joined.

items.followUp: How does cytokinesis take place in an animal cell during mitosis?

rubric.why: Identifies how and where the plant cell plate begins to form.
rubric.description: Golgi-derived vesicles gather and fuse at the equator to form a cell plate.
rubric.how: Award for stating that a cell plate forms at the equator; vesicles are an acceptable added detail.

rubric.why: Explains how the cell plate completes division.
rubric.description: The cell plate grows outwards and joins the existing cell wall, separating the two daughter cells.
rubric.how: Award for describing the cell plate growing to divide the cell.

modelAnswer: Golgi-derived vesicles gather at the equator of the plant cell and fuse to form a cell plate.
The cell plate grows outwards and joins the existing cell wall, dividing the cytoplasm into two daughter cells.

items.followUp: What happens to the rate of photosynthesis when light intensity increases, and why does it eventually level off?

rubric.why: States the effect of increasing carbon dioxide concentration when it is limiting.
rubric.description: Increasing carbon dioxide concentration increases the rate of photosynthesis.
rubric.how: Award for the increase in rate as carbon dioxide concentration rises.

rubric.why: States the limit to the effect of carbon dioxide concentration.
rubric.description: At a certain concentration the rate reaches a maximum and levels off because another factor becomes limiting.
rubric.how: Award for identifying the plateau and a limiting factor.

modelAnswer: As carbon dioxide concentration increases, the rate of photosynthesis increases, provided carbon dioxide is a limiting factor.
At a certain concentration the rate reaches a maximum and levels off because another factor becomes limiting.

items.followUp: How is lactic acid produced in muscle cells when oxygen is insufficient?

rubric.why: Identifies the conversion involved in lactic acid fermentation.
rubric.description: When oxygen is insufficient, pyruvate is converted into lactic acid in skeletal muscle cells.
rubric.how: Award for stating that pyruvate or pyruvic acid is converted to lactic acid.

rubric.why: Explains the anaerobic context or the role of fermentation in continuing glycolysis.
rubric.description: This process regenerates NAD⁺, allowing glycolysis to continue and release a small amount of ATP.
rubric.how: Award for linking the process to oxygen shortage or continued glycolysis through NAD⁺ regeneration.

modelAnswer: When oxygen is insufficient, pyruvate formed during glycolysis is converted into lactic acid in skeletal muscle cells.
This regenerates NAD⁺, allowing glycolysis to continue and release a small amount of ATP.

items.followUp: Name one use of enzymes in the textile industry.

rubric.why: States the main paper-industry application of enzymes.
rubric.description: Enzymes are used to remove ink from recycled paper during de-inking.
rubric.how: Award both marks for identifying enzymatic de-inking of recycled paper.

modelAnswer: Enzymes are mainly used to remove ink from recycled paper during the de-inking process.

items.followUp: What is an enzyme activator, and how can it affect enzyme activity?

rubric.why: Defines cofactors by their non-protein nature and role in enzyme function.
rubric.description: Cofactors are non-protein components required for the activity of some enzymes.
rubric.how: Award for identifying a cofactor as a non-protein component needed for enzyme activity.

rubric.why: Distinguishes coenzymes from cofactors in general.
rubric.description: Coenzymes are organic cofactors, often derived from vitamins, that assist enzyme activity.
rubric.how: Award for identifying coenzymes as organic cofactors.

modelAnswer: Cofactors are non-protein components required for the activity of some enzymes; they may be inorganic ions or organic molecules.
Coenzymes are organic cofactors, often derived from vitamins, that assist enzyme activity.
